The Barn swallow (Hirundo rustica) initiates reproduction relatively early in life compared to other migratory passerines. Following their arrival at breeding grounds in the spring, first-year birds typically commence their first breeding attempt approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching], a timeline that aligns with their annual migratory cycle at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. During the peak of the breeding season, when ambient conditions correspond to an internal body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], females produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], each containing between 4 and 5 eggs [N_R_i = each containing between 4 and 5 eggs]. This reproductive schedule yields a substantial annual output that is critical for population maintenance in the face of high predation pressure on nests. The energetic demands of such repeated laying events are considerable, especially given that females must also invest heavily in incubation and subsequent provisioning of altricial young. The timing of this first brood is tightly linked to the seasonal abundance of aerial insect prey, ensuring that peak food availability coincides with the nestling period, thereby maximizing the probability of fledging success for the initial cohort of the season.

Upon hatching, which occurs after an incubation period of approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days] at a nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the altricial nestlings emerge completely dependent on parental care. These neonates possess an initial wet weight at birth of only 1.3 grams [Wwb = 1.3 grams], a minute mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available in the passerine egg. This low birth mass necessitates an intense period of rapid somatic growth, fueled almost entirely by the parents' relentless foraging efforts. The newly hatched chicks are blind and naked, relying entirely on the brooding warmth provided by the female to maintain their body temperature until their own thermoregulatory capacities develop. The comparatively brief incubation period, ranging between 14 and 19 days in most studies, is characteristic of smaller Hirundinidae and represents a trade-off between minimizing exposure of the eggs to predation and ensuring sufficient embryonic development for the chick to survive the hatching process and the subsequent critical early days of life.

The nestling period of the Barn swallow is characterized by a dramatic transformation in body size and physiological capacity. Under the thermal conditions typical of an active, metabolically demanding passerine, around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the young grow toward an ultimate wet weight of 27 grams [Wwi = 27 grams], which represents the asymptotic mass they achieve before fledging. This adult-like mass, however, is often slightly higher than the mean mass of breeding adults, as individuals typically undergo a period of weight loss during the energetically costly reproductive season. The growth trajectory from a 1.3 gram hatchling to a 27 gram fledgling requires a massive intake of insect prey, primarily Diptera, that is delivered by both parents with remarkable frequency. This rapid mass gain is paralleled by the development of the flight feathers and the strengthening of the pectoral muscles, both of which are essential for the upcoming transition to independent flight and foraging. The rate of this growth is sensitive to food availability, with chicks in poor years often failing to reach the full asymptotic mass before fledging.

Fledging represents a critical developmental milestone for the young Barn swallow, marking their departure from the nest and the commencement of aerial life. At a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], typical of an endothermic bird at rest, the time since birth at fledging is approximately 20 days [tx = approximately 20 days], a relatively short nestling duration that is typical of many small passerines. This period, which can range from 18 to 23 days depending on local conditions and food supply, ends with the young taking their first flight. Immediately after fledging, the young birds are still dependent on their parents for food as they learn to catch insects on the wing, a skill that requires considerable practice. The onset of puberty, which defines the achievement of full sexual maturity, is reached at a time since birth of approximately 60 days [tp = approximately 60 days], although most individuals will not breed until the following spring. at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]This gap between physiological maturation and actual first reproduction is a common life-history strategy in migratory species, allowing young birds to refine their foraging skills and build the necessary body condition for the rigors of migration and nesting.

The Barn swallow exhibits a relatively short maximum lifespan for a bird of its size, a characteristic shaped by the high mortality associated with long-distance migration and the risks of colonial nesting. The oldest documented individuals in the wild have been recorded surviving for up to 16 years [am = up to 16 years], a considerable age given the annual hazards they face, though such longevity is exceptional compared to other Hirundinidae of similar bod at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]y mass. This maximum lifespan is achieved only by individuals that successfully navigate the perils of multiple trans-Saharan migrations and avoid predation at the nest site. In terms of egg dimensions, the eggs themselves are striking in their size relative to the female's body mass, measuring approximately 2 centimeters in length and 1.37 centimeters in width. Calculating the weight of a typical egg using the formula for a prolate spheroid gives a value of approximately 1.97 grams, a figure that slightly exceeds the mass of the newborn chick itself, reflecting the substantial albumen and yolk resources that must be converted into tissue during incubation.
